9662:90.gloss: Hume defines a miracle here as a violation of a law of nature by the will of God or of some invisible agent, and states his maxim: testimony can establish a miracle only if its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event it reports. Told that a dead man was restored to life, he weighs the chance that the witness deceives or is deceived against the event itself, and rejects whichever would be the greater miracle. The page ends as Part II opens, where he argues that even this concession was too generous.

quotes.text: no testimony is sufficient to establish a miracle, unless the testimony be of such a kind, that its falsehood would be more miraculous, than the fact
I weigh the one miracle against the other; and according to the superiority, which I discover, I pronounce my decision, and always reject the greater miracle.

57359:345.gloss: Venn finishes an argument about several witnesses: when they could have erred in many different ways, their agreement raises the likelihood of the event enormously, but only if collusion is ruled out, which in practice it seldom can be, so he judges combined testimony even less fit for calculation than single testimony. Section 21 then turns to miraculous stories, which he holds cannot be adequately treated by the rules of probability, and starts by looking for a definition of a miracle.

quotes.text: the combination of their favourable testimony adds enormously to the likelihood of the event; provided always that there is no chance of collusion
The impossibility of any adequate or even appropriate consideration of the credibility of miraculous stories by the rules of Probability has been already noticed

58881:78.gloss: Laplace uses the Port-Royal cure of 1656 to show how general opinion sways even great minds: Racine reported the recovery of Pascal's niece as miraculous, and Pascal argued that the miracle was needed to vindicate the monks of the abbey. He adds that miracles and sorcery did not yet seem improbable in that century, and cites Locke's view that a fair testimony can win assent even to supernatural events, which Laplace treats as a misunderstanding of how testimonies should be weighed.

quotes.text: At this time miracles and sorcery did not yet appear improbable
The true principles of the probability of testimonies having been thus misunderstood
